current.rappels: One rappel of about 30 m from a slung horn at the top of the crux pitch (a 60 m rope doubled), then downclimb the loose gully; or downclimb the whole route

rappel_detail.notes: The one standard rappel, about 30 m on a 60 m rope doubled (or two ropes tied), back onto the southwest face gully. Then downclimb the loose gully to the base.
rappel_detail.anchor: rock horn with slings and rap rings (natural, not bolted)
hazards: Very loose rock throughout; stagger the party through the gully and wear helmets.
rappel_detail.station: The top of the exposed crux pitch on the southwest face, reached by downclimbing from the summit block to the ridge crest.

current.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit block back to the ridge crest, then descend the southwest face on the same line used to climb it. At the top of the exposed crux pitch (the awkward-angle pitch most parties rope up for on the way up), the standard descent is one double-rope rappel — parties describe a rock horn near the top rigged with slings and rap rings from prior parties, used as the anchor (natural horn/sling anchor, not bolted). Bring a single 60m rope doubled, or two ropes tied together, to make the ~30m rappel back down onto the SW face/gully; from there, downclimb the loose gully back to the base of the buttress. A minority of parties instead descend via the Northwest Couloir to avoid re-downclimbing the exposed ascent terrain, but that is a variation rather than the standard descent line, and its rappel/anchor situation is not well known — treat it as an alpine-judgment call, not a known bail route. From the base of the rock, retrace the scramble approach back to the Cathedral Pass/PCT junction and follow the maintained Cathedral Rock Trail back to the trailhead. Primary descent hazards are loose rock, very loose everywhere, and rockfall onto parties below — helmets are essentially mandatory, and stagger the group through the gully.

current.rappels: 2 double-rope (60m) rappels from slung horns (first from just below the summit to a horn at the top of pitch 2, second back to the base)
current.rappel_count_note: Two rappels, and this count assumes two 60 m ropes doubled through natural horn anchors — that is the published kit for the route and a single rope does not link the stations. Both anchors are slung granite horns rather than fixed hardware, so carry replacement webbing. Per-station distances are not published, so none is listed.

rappel_detail.pull: Two 60 m ropes are the standard kit for this descent and a single rope will not link these two stations. Pull the strands clear of the horn so they do not wrap it.
rappel_detail.notes: First double-rope rappel from the summit area down to the large slung horn at the top of pitch 2.
rappel_detail.anchor: large granite horn with sling anchor
hazards: The downclimb from the notch to the horn crosses loose blocks and broken corners; it is short but it is where the descent's rockfall risk is concentrated.
The station is whatever tat is currently around the horn. Carry webbing and a ring so you can replace rather than rappel on faded slings.
rappel_detail.station: From the bunny-ears notch at the top of the route, downclimb about 5 m (15 ft) to the next ledge down. The anchor is fixed slings around a large granite horn — a natural anchor, not hardware. The rappel from it runs on doubled 60 m ropes to a second large slung horn at the top of pitch 2.

rappel_detail.pull: Straight down the face to the scree; stand out from the base of the wall when pulling.
rappel_detail.notes: Second double-rope rappel completes the descent to the scree base.
hazards: Second natural horn anchor with no fixed hardware; inspect and back up before the last person goes.
Loose rock across the face means anything the ropes sweep off lands at the base of the route where packs and other parties are.
rappel_detail.station: The large slung horn at the top of pitch 2 — the same kind of natural station as the first, and the one you land on from above. The second doubled rappel from it returns you to the scree at the base of the East Face.

current.descent_text: From the summit area, downclimb via loose blocks and corners to locate the large granite horn with established sling anchor. This is a critical waypoint. Thread both 60m ropes through the horn slings. First double-rope rappel descends to the large slung horn at the top of pitch 2. Reanchor ropes there for the second rappel to complete descent to scree base of East Face. Exercise caution for rockfall and loose rock throughout the descent process.

current.rappels: Typically a single 60m rappel (occasionally two) through the summit gully/notch back into the basin; some late-day/crowded ascents have required additional downclimbing when rope length fell short
current.rappel_count_note: The two counts on this page are the same descent with a different rope setup, not a disagreement. The gully on the south side of the east face goes in one 60 m double-rope rappel, or in the two ~30 m single-rope rappels listed here. How much you rappel at all depends on conditions: with good steep snow much of it is downclimbed, and parties describe reaching the base on a single rappel plus downclimbing. Two rappel stations were added in early summer 2023 so that a 60 m rope makes every rappel on the route - several leave under 5 ft of rope spare, so knot the ends.

rappel_detail.notes: First of two double-rope (60m) rappels; some downclimbing needed to reach the next station.
rappel_detail.anchor: trees/rock horn near head of gully

rappel_detail.notes: Second double-rope rappel reaching easier snow near the gully's base.

current.descent_text: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.

current.rappels: 1-2 rope-length rappels (up to 60m) through the cornice-prone SW-facing exit gully, combined with downclimbing
current.rappel_count_note: One rappel on the standard descent, from the fixed piton station in the first gully on climber's left. Two ropes clear the corniced lip in a single 60 m rappel; a single 60 m rope halves it and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb. The second descent gully is an alternative rather than a continuation — it carries both an upper and a lower anchor, so one rope suffices there. Rappelling the buttress itself in summer is a separate option again, taking four to five shorter rappels.

rappel_detail.pull: Ropes have hung up on retrieval — one party's jammed, they judged the rope had cut into the snow, and freed it only by repeated hauling. Test the pull before the next person commits.
rappel_detail.notes: The anchor is fixed and old; a knife and 20 ft of cord will let you re-rig it. Two ropes give one 60 m rappel that clears the cornice and lands where the gully opens out and ends. A single 60 m rope halves that and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb, still fully in the fall line — a tag line buys a quick rappel to a protected stance instead of a long spell standing in it.
rappel_detail.anchor: three fixed pitons tied together with aging webbing and two aluminium rappel rings
rappel_detail.hazards: The lip is often heavily corniced and the rappel goes through a gap in the cornice. Sloughs run the gully in warm conditions and you are exposed to overhead hazard for the whole of it. Once down, move to the side of the gully mouth so the next person cannot drop anything on you; close calls from rock knocked down by a party behind are on record here.
rappel_detail.station: Coming off the flat top of the peak, drop into the first obvious gully on climber's left — not the one further along the ridge near the true summit. Old tat on two small trees marks the entrance. The gully runs due south between high rock walls: scramble down and take the very first left it offers, and the anchor comes into view as soon as the walls let you out, at roughly 6,000 ft. Parties miss it by carrying on too far down, or too far right, once the gully opens up.

current.descent_text:
From the top of the buttress, scramble back across the flat summit area and drop into the first obvious gully on climber's left — not the gully further along the ridge near the true summit. Old tat on two small trees marks the entrance. The gully runs due south between high rock walls: scramble down it and take the very first left it offers, and the rappel station comes into view as soon as the walls let you out, at roughly 6,000 ft. Parties miss it by carrying on too far down, or too far right, once the gully opens up.

The station is fixed and old — three rusty pitons tied together with a mass of aging webbing and a pair of aluminium rappel rings. Two ropes give a single 60 m rappel that clears the corniced lip and lands where the gully opens out and ends; a single 60 m rope halves that and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb, still fully exposed to whatever comes down the gully. Move to the side of the gully mouth once you are down so the next person cannot drop anything on you. A tag line is worth carrying for exactly that reason — it buys a quick rappel to a protected stance instead of a long spell standing in the fall line.

A second gully further along is an alternative rather than a continuation: it carries both an upper and a lower anchor, so a single rope is enough to get through that one instead. Anchors on this descent are not maintained and may not be where you want them — carry cord and a knife to re-rig, and expect that getting around remaining steep snow at the base may take an extra downclimb or rappel.

Below the rappel, plunge-step or downclimb 35-40° snow to the base of the east face and traverse east to rejoin the approach. Cornice collapse at the gully lip, sloughing in warm conditions, and rock knocked down by parties above are the main descent hazards.

Rappelling the buttress itself is a documented summer alternative, taking four to five shorter rappels off a tree, a second gnarlier tree, an old pair of bolts and a rock horn.

current.rappels: Rappel the route on fixed anchors, generally trending climber's right; two 60m ropes recommended. Parties describe roughly 4 double-rope rappels from the summit block back to the base (first from the summit block, second from the top of the P5 crux pitch, remaining down slabby terrain to the glacier/snow).
current.rappel_count_note: Four double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes from the summit block back to the snow, trending to the rappeller's right. A single 60 m rope may reach some stations but is not the norm. Individual lengths are not published.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 4 on two 60 m ropes, trending to the rappeller's right.
rappel_detail.anchor: two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block
hazards: Check the fixed anchor before weighting it.
rappel_detail.station: The southeast base of the summit block, reached by scrambling down from the summit pedestal.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull carefully: the flake and offwidth features snag ropes readily.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 4 on two ropes, continuing to the right.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed anchor at the top of the pitch-5 crux
hazards: Rope snags in the chimney and offwidth sections.
rappel_detail.station: The top of the crux fifth pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 4 on two ropes down slabby terrain.
rappel_detail.station: A fixed station lower on the face, on the slabbier ground to climber's right of the route.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 4 of 4, to the snow at the base of the face; collect any gear left there and reverse the snow traverse to Burgundy Col.
rappel_detail.station: The lowest fixed station on the face.

current.descent_text: Same descent as the standard East Face/Rebel Yell line: rappel back down the route itself on fixed anchors rather than walking off. The usual descent is four double-rope rappels using two ropes (a single 60m may work for some stations but isn't the norm), starting from the summit block, then anchors near the top of pitch 5, then continuing stations down the route generally trending climber's-right. Anchors are fixed but should be visually checked each time — this isn't a heavily-bolted sport-style descent. Rope-snag hazard exists in the chimney/offwidth pitches. After reaching the base, reverse the Silver Star Glacier traverse and snow step back to Burgundy Col, then descend the climber's trail to Early Winters Creek and the highway — parties describe this exit as notably long and tiring relative to the climb, so plan daylight accordingly.

current.rappels: 4 double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes down the neighbouring Rebel Yell line, from the two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block; or reverse to the Burgundy-Chianti notch

current.descent_text: Most parties on the east face descend the way Rebel Yell parties do: from the summit pedestal, scramble to the two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block and make four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes back to the snow at the base of the face, trending generally to the rappeller's right and pulling the ropes carefully - the flake and offwidth features snag ropes readily. The alternative, and the one this route's finish naturally suggests, is to reverse to the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti and descend from there. Either way, collect gear left at the base, reverse the snow traverse north beneath Burgundy Spire's east face, and regain the 200-300 ft to Burgundy Col - much easier on firm snow than late-day slush or bare sand. Then descend the loose main gully (helmets on), rejoin the trail at the bench, and take the steep path down to Early Winters Creek, finishing with the short loose scramble back up to the highway. The sandy slabs above the bench are the most-cursed section of the whole outing; trekking poles help.

current.rappels: 1 short rappel or downclimb off the summit block, from an old bolt, then reverse the route to the Burgundy-Chianti notch; bring two ropes only if rappelling the east face instead

rappel_detail.notes: One short rappel, or a downclimb, off the summit block back onto the north face. Then reverse the line to the Burgundy-Chianti notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: an old bolt on top of the summit block; back it up
rappel_detail.station: The top of Chianti's summit block.

current.descent_text: Downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block back onto the north face, then reverse the line to the Burgundy-Chianti notch. From the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy Spire's east face and climb the 200-300 ft back up to Burgundy Col - this re-ascent is the sting in the tail and is much easier on firm morning snow than on afternoon slush or bare, sandy rock. From the col, descend the main gully carefully; below the bench the trail is fast but relentlessly steep, and the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway is a short, loose scramble on scree and boulders. Trip reports are unanimous that the sand-over-slab descent above the bench is the worst part of the day; trekking poles help enormously, and a helmet should stay on because parties above you dislodge rocks in the gullies.
